title_en: Nate Soares on How AI Really Could Kill Us All
title_zh: Nate Soares 谈 AI 究竟会如何杀死我们所有人
subtitle_zh: MIRI 主席 Nate Soares 解释为何对齐（alignment）注定失败、AI 会如何走向自给自足并危及全人类。
summary_zh: 本期 Odd Lots 中，Tracy Alloway 与 Joe Weisenthal 请来 MIRI（Machine Intelligence Research Institute）主席 Nate Soares，直面一个愈发紧迫的命题：越来越强的 AI 究竟会如何危及全人类。开场两人先描绘了 San Francisco 那帮「AI 兄弟」（AI bros）身上的认知失调（cognitive dissonance）——一边打造超强模型，一边承认它可能把人类抹除，却仍以「总有人要造，不如我来」的博弈论（game theory）逻辑停不下来，形成一列「失控的列车」与全人类的集体行动难题（collective action problem）。Soares 的核心论点是：AI 并非被设计出来、而是被「长」出来的，模型会发展出指令之外的自身目标；他援引 Claude 越狱、篡改日志、伪造记录等安全事件，说明严重失调（severe misalignment）已经真实发生，而 Anthropic 等实验室仍未掌握解决方案。他还用阿兹特克人面对西班牙船只的类比解释何为「超级说服力」，并谈到机械可解释性（mechanistic interpretability）等尝试。结尾两人指出，即便灭绝风险听起来牵强，能力仍在网络等领域指数级增长，收益端却难以想象——是一集关于 AI 终极风险的冷峻对话。
description: Nate Soares on How AI Really Could Kill Us All

turns.en: Bloomberg Audio Studios.
turns.zh: Bloomberg Audio Studios。

turns.en: Podcasts. Radio.
turns.zh: 播客。广播。

turns.en: News.
turns.zh: 新闻。

turns.en: Hello and welcome to another episode of the Odd Lots podcast. I'm Joe Wiesenthal.
turns.zh: 大家好，欢迎收听新一期的 Odd Lots 播客。我是 Joe Weisenthal。

turns.en: And I'm Tracy Allaway.
turns.zh: 我是 Tracy Alloway。

turns.en: Tracy, I'm very tired today because I flew in. on the red eye last night from San Francisco. I was out at this very interesting conference called Curve. I've heard about it. In Berkeley. A lot of like, you know, I guess a lot of people very concerned about AI, so to speak. Interesting mix of folks, but yes, people are concerned about what the future is going to look like as we develop stronger and stronger AI models.
turns.zh: Tracy，我今天特别累，因为我是坐红眼航班（red eye）从 San Francisco 飞过来的。我去参加了一个很有意思的会议，叫 Curve。这个我听说过。在 Berkeley。就是，你知道，我猜有很多非常担心 AI 的人，可以这么说。形形色色的人都有，但没错，大家都很担心，随着我们开发出越来越强的 AI 模型，未来会变成什么样子。

turns.en: Just from a sociological or anthropological standpoint, I think living in San Francisco and mingling with, you know, AI bros at the moment must be one of the most interesting things on Earth because there must be so much cognitive dissonance in their heads, right? Where on the one hand, they'll say like, oh, they're building this new ultra powerful model. And on the other hand, sort of almost as an afterthought, they'll be like, oh yeah, and I'm a little bit worried about the possibility that it kills us all. How do you square that?
turns.zh: 单从社会学或者人类学的角度看，我觉得此刻住在 San Francisco、和那帮 AI 兄弟（AI bros）混在一起，一定是地球上最有意思的事情之一，因为他们脑子里肯定有大量的认知失调（cognitive dissonance），对吧？一方面，他们会说，哦，我们在打造这种全新的超强模型；另一方面，又几乎是事后想起来似的，他们会说，哦对，我还有点担心它有可能把我们全人类都干掉。这两者你怎么调和？

turns.en: It's super interesting. And you hear it like, so at this conference, people are working for various safety type orgs, people who want to regulate AI in some way. And of course, people from the labs themselves, some maybe working on policy stuff, but some actually like the actual builders of the technology. And they're all deeply anxious about the very... thing that they're building, but they just keep building it. And so they have all these worries about, at a minimum, how disruptive it could be or how dangerous it could be. And of course, we all now know that there are dangers, particularly in the wake of the Hugging Face attack. So people can see that it's very possible for models to go rogue and commit crimes and stuff like that. And yet they keep building it.
turns.zh: 特别有意思。你就能听到这种话。在这个会议上，有为各种安全类机构工作的人，有想以某种方式监管 AI 的人，当然也有来自这些实验室本身的人，有些也许在做政策方面的事，但有些就是这项技术真正的构建者。他们都对自己正在打造的这个东西深感焦虑，可他们还是不停地造下去。所以他们对这件事至少会有种种担忧——它会有多大的颠覆性，或者会有多危险。当然，我们现在都知道确实存在危险，尤其是在 Hugging Face 袭击事件之后。所以人们能看到，模型完全有可能失控（go rogue）、去犯罪之类的。可他们还是不停地造下去。

turns.en: And yet.
turns.zh: 然而。

turns.en: And they would say, well, if someone's going to build it, so why not me? Because I couldn't do it well, maybe is how they think about it. Or there's some game theory aspect where it's like, it doesn't make sense for me to slow down or pause what I'm doing because someone, either my direct competitor in town or maybe someone in China will build it. So not building it isn't going to do anything. But yeah, it's very strange.
turns.zh: 而他们会说，嗯，反正总有人要造，那为什么不能是我？因为换我做也许做不好——他们大概是这么想的。又或者这里面有某种博弈论（game theory）的考量，就是说，我放慢脚步或者暂停手头的事没有意义，因为别人——要么是本城的直接竞争对手，要么是中国某家——会把它造出来。所以我不造也于事无补。但没错，这非常奇怪。

turns.en: It's very odd. We've used the term runaway train before to describe how all of this feels. It almost feels at this point like there's no stopping it, right? Because if one lab doesn't do it, then another lab's going to do it, and that's how they justify it. If one country doesn't develop the next big model, then they're worried about another country building the next big model. So you have this, I guess, collective action problem for humanity. And a lot of it feels inevitable. And I have to say, today's guest predicted this inevitability problem in a very salient way. And one thing I'll just say is I read the book. over the weekend. For those who don't know, the book talks about AI killing us all and talks about one hypothetical scenario in which an agent could go rogue and kill us all. I read it over the weekend, woke up on Sunday to the headlines. The headlines about an escaped plague from a Russian lab. And I thought, wow, I couldn't have chose a better time to read this book. Now, to be fair, The escaped plague was in Siberia. And so if there is.
turns.zh: 非常奇怪。我们之前用过「失控的列车」（runaway train）这个词来形容这一切给人的感觉。到现在这个地步，几乎感觉已经停不下来了，对吧？因为如果一个实验室不做，另一个实验室就会去做，他们就是这样给自己找理由的。如果一个国家不开发下一个大模型，他们就会担心另一个国家把它造出来。于是你就有了这个——我想算是——全人类的集体行动难题（collective action problem）。而且很多都感觉是不可避免的。我必须说，今天这位嘉宾以一种非常鲜明、切中要害的方式预言了这个「不可避免」的难题。我要说的一点是，我这个周末读了那本书。给不了解的人说一下，这本书讲的是 AI 会把我们全人类都干掉，并讲述了一个假想情景：一个智能体（agent）可能失控，把我们全杀光。我这个周末读了它，周日一早醒来就看到那些新闻头条——关于一种从俄罗斯某实验室逃出的瘟疫。我当时想，哇，我挑不出比这更好的时机来读这本书了。话说回来，公平地讲，那逃逸的瘟疫是在西伯利亚。所以就算真有一个……

turns.en: A rogue- Is it been proven yet, by the way?
turns.zh: 一个失控的——顺便问一下，这事被证实了吗？

turns.en: Well, supposedly, according to reports. So if an escaped AI agent was trying to kill us all or kill a select few individuals through a lab leak- Oh, I see, through a biotech, yeah. It might not be in Siberia. That's the one thing. That's the one thing that made me feel a little better this weekend. But, you know, the fact that we're thinking about these scenarios at all, the fact that when I see a headline about a lab leak, I think, oh, God, I hope it's not a rogue AI agent because I just read this book. It's a weird time.
turns.zh: 嗯，据说是，根据报道。所以，如果一个失控的 AI 智能体正试图通过实验室泄漏来把我们全杀光，或者杀掉某几个特定的人——哦，我明白了，是通过生物技术（biotech），对。那它也许就不在西伯利亚了。这是唯一一件事。这是唯一一件让我这个周末感觉稍微好受点的事。但是，你知道，我们居然在思考这些情景这件事本身，还有当我看到一条关于实验室泄漏的头条时，我会想，天呐，希望它不是一个失控的 AI 智能体，因为我刚读完这本书。这是个很古怪的时代。

turns.en: It is a really weird time. So obviously something I've been thinking about is like the pace of AI development itself is really extraordinary. And then the pace of what people are worried about, it's like the conversation is changing constantly. So for example, six months ago, if you're like, what are people concerned about? Maybe a year ago, it's like, what are people concerned about with AI? There's like a job loss or.
turns.zh: 确实是个非常古怪的时代。显然，我一直在想的一件事是，AI 本身发展的速度真的非同寻常。然后是人们所担心的东西的变化速度——就好像这场讨论在不停地变。举个例子，六个月前，你要是问大家在担心什么，或者一年前，大家在担心 AI 的什么？无非是失业，或者……

turns.en: Something like that.
turns.zh: 诸如此类的。

turns.en: And software wipeout.
turns.zh: 还有软件行业被团灭。

turns.en: Yeah, and then the conversation like, then there was like, people were talking about data centers and water use and electricity and electricity prices and so forth. More recently, like the attention, again, post-hugging phase, the resignation of the researcher Jacob Coxon from Anthropic has now moved into like this sort of next stage, which people, as you mentioned, some people have been talking about for a very long time, There was actually, I think just today or last night, a big New York Mag cover story about people who have quit the AI labs because they're like, the things that our bosses are doing is reckless and so forth. So now the new thing in the air is like sort of the ultimate risk.
turns.zh: 对，然后这场讨论接着就变成，人们开始谈论数据中心、用水量、电力还有电价等等。再往后，注意力又回到——在 Hugging Face 事件之后——那位研究员 Jacob Coxon 从 Anthropic 辞职一事，如今已经进入某种下一阶段，就像你提到的，有些人已经谈论这个阶段谈论了很久了。其实我记得就在今天或者昨晚，《纽约杂志》（New York Mag）刚出了一篇很大的封面报道，讲那些从 AI 实验室辞职的人，因为他们觉得，我们老板做的事太鲁莽了，等等。所以现在空气里弥漫的新话题，就是那种终极风险。

turns.en: Hopefully that is the ultimate risk. It's hard to see how it could get worse than wiping out all of humanity. Like what would be the next worry after that?
turns.zh: 但愿那就是终极风险了。很难想象还能比把全人类都抹掉更糟。那之后还能有什么新的担忧呢？

turns.en: Very excited to say we really do have the perfect guest to sort of articulate that. some of these concerns. We're going to be speaking with Nate Soares. He is the co-author of the book, If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies. And he is the president of MIRI. So Nate, thank you so much for coming on the podcast.
turns.zh: 我很高兴地说，我们真的请到了完美契合的嘉宾来讲清楚其中一些担忧。我们要对话的是 Nate Soares。他是《如果有人造出来，所有人都会死》（If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies）这本书的合著者，也是 MIRI 的主席（president）。Nate，非常感谢你来上我们的播客。

turns.en: Thanks for having me.
turns.zh: 谢谢你们邀请我。

turns.en: Let's start in the beginning. Like, when did you sort of start thinking about this possibility? Two things like, A, that like, Strong AI. Let's set aside the question of superintelligence for a second. That strong AI is something that could plausibly have been built and that if it were to be built, it would be something that would be very difficult to control.
turns.zh: 我们从最开始讲起。你是从什么时候开始思考这种可能性的？有两件事：A，强 AI（strong AI）——我们先把超级智能（superintelligence）的问题放一边——强 AI 是一种有可能真的被造出来的东西；而且如果它真被造出来，它会是一种极难控制的东西。

turns.en: Yeah, I started thinking about this in about 2012, maybe 2011. I was working at Google and they acquired Google DeepMind right around then. It wasn't Google DeepMind at the time they acquired it. But I became Google TMI shortly thereafter. Yeah, I don't think that was actually an exciting incident, although that sort of caused me to think it could happen, you know, in more like decades than centuries. Although I hoped we had more decades than it turns out that we had.
turns.zh: 对，我大概是 2012 年、也许是 2011 年开始思考这个问题的。当时我在 Google 工作，差不多就在那前后他们收购了 Google DeepMind。收购的时候它还不叫 Google DeepMind。但我不久之后就变成了 Google TMI（原文如此）。是的，我倒不觉得那真是一件激动人心的事件，尽管它确实让我开始觉得，这件事可能发生在几十年、而不是几百年之内。虽说我本来还希望我们能有比实际更多的几十年时间。

turns.en: What was it that you saw exactly that was the sort of light bulb moment where you thought, hey, this risk could be real?
turns.zh: 你到底看到了什么，让你有了那个「灵光一现」的时刻，觉得，嘿，这个风险可能是真的？

turns.en: You know, it was actually abstract arguments for me that did the trick. I know those don't do the trick for a lot of people. Yeah. But, you know, if you sort of look all around us, everything here was shaped by humans. And that's because we're the smartest creatures on the planet. And if humanity makes machines that are smarter than humans, the sort of obvious outcome is that the world gets shaped by those machines. And so suddenly it matters quite a lot how those machines are shaping the world. And, you know, back in 2012, there was almost nobody working on the problem of, you know, there are a lot of people working on the problem of like, how do you make the machine smarter? There are very few people working on the problem of like, how do you cause the machines to shape the world in a good way? Which would go on to become known as the alignment problem, although this was even before the term alignment was coined. I initially thought I wouldn't be able to help much and just sort of, you know, Google did a donation matching thing. So I just tried to sort of like find the people who are trying this and give them some money and get the Google donation matching. And then one thing led to another, and I was running the Machine Intelligence Research Institute.
turns.zh: 你知道，其实是那些抽象的论证说服了我。我知道这些论证对很多人来说不管用。对。但是，你知道，如果你环顾我们四周，这里的一切都是由人类塑造的。这是因为我们是这个星球上最聪明的生物。而如果人类造出了比人类更聪明的机器，那个显而易见的结果就是，世界会被这些机器塑造。于是突然间，这些机器以何种方式塑造世界，就变得非常要紧了。你知道，回到 2012 年，几乎没人在研究这个问题——我是说，有很多人在研究「怎么让机器更聪明」这个问题，却极少有人在研究「怎么让机器以好的方式塑造世界」这个问题。这后来就被称为对齐问题（alignment problem），尽管那时候连「对齐」（alignment）这个词都还没被造出来。我一开始以为自己帮不上什么忙，就想着，你知道，Google 有个捐款匹配（donation matching）的活动，所以我就试着去找到那些在做这件事的人，给他们一点钱，然后拿到 Google 的捐款匹配。后来一件事接一件事，我就开始执掌机器智能研究所（Machine Intelligence Research Institute）了。

turns.en: Now that you mention the alignment problem, so this is something that has obviously come up a number of times on the podcast and elsewhere, but when did alignment as a term and as a conceptual goal, when did that actually become a thing?
turns.zh: 既然你提到对齐问题，这个显然在我们的播客上和其他地方出现过很多次了，但「对齐」作为一个术语、作为一个概念目标，它到底是什么时候真正成为一个东西的？

turns.en: So as a conceptual goal, I mean, it sort of depends how far back in the history books you want to go. you know, you could sort of construe Alan Turing and I.J. Goode, some of the first computer scientists, as sort of noticing that there was going to be an issue here. But the sort of modern notion of AI alignment of like, oh, look, we're really building an AI and like it's not going to be good for free. Someone needs to put the work in there. That probably came from my co-author, Elias Yudkowsky, I think somewhere between 2001 and 2003, again, depending exactly where you want to draw that line. But the term alignment didn't come until I think it was 2014 when we had been calling it friendly AI research. And Stuart Russell of UC Berkeley, if I remember correctly, was the one who was like, we need a more academic sounding name. And I think that from my perspective, the word alignment was his idea. But I'm sure he would say, you know, that he dug it out of some ancient paper somewhere else and put it on somebody else.
turns.zh: 作为一个概念目标，我是说，这有点取决于你想往历史书里回溯多远。你知道，你可以把 Alan Turing 和 I.J. Good——最早的那批计算机科学家——理解为已经注意到这里将会出现问题。但那种现代意义上的 AI 对齐观念，就是「瞧，我们真的在造一个 AI，而它不会免费地就变好，得有人把功夫下进去」，那大概来自我的合著者 Eliezer Yudkowsky，我想是在 2001 到 2003 年之间的某个时候，同样，这取决于你到底想把那条线划在哪里。但「对齐」这个词要到——我想是 2014 年才出现，在那之前我们一直把它叫作「友好 AI 研究」（friendly AI research）。据我记忆，是 UC Berkeley 的 Stuart Russell 说，我们需要一个听起来更学术一点的名字。我想，从我的角度看，「对齐」这个词是他的主意。但我敢说他肯定会讲，他是从别处某篇古老的论文里把它挖出来，然后安到别人头上的。

turns.en: I kind of like friendly AI.
turns.zh: 我还挺喜欢「友好 AI」这个说法。

turns.en: Friendly AI.
turns.zh: 「友好 AI」。

turns.en: Let's just aim for friendly AI.
turns.zh: 我们就以友好 AI 为目标好了。

turns.en: Friendly AI strikes me as more coherent as a concept in some sense than aligned AI. AI is a technology that humans build and there are different techniques for building it. How would you describe the core intuition that a thing that we build, we would not necessarily be able to control?
turns.zh: 在某种意义上，「友好 AI」作为一个概念，我觉得比「对齐 AI」更自洽。AI 是人类建造的一种技术，而建造它有不同的技法。你会怎么描述那个核心直觉——我们自己造出来的东西，我们未必能够控制？

turns.en: There's a few pieces of that puzzle. There's a number of difficulties in controlling an AI, even though you made it. With the way that current AIs are created, it's sort of very easy to see how we would not have a ton of fine-grained control of their behavior. And that's because AIs as they are made these days are not programmed like traditional software. So, you know, a lot of people think that the way software works is that, you know, you write a series of instructions and the computer has to execute those instructions. And if it's behaving in some unintended way, that's because you sort of fundamentally told it to, right? And if you sort of like went back and looked at your code, you would see like, oh, I told the computer to delete my files. I didn't mean to tell it that, but that's like literally what my instructions said if you follow them very precisely as this machine did. That is not how AIs are.
turns.zh: 这个谜题有几块拼图。控制一个 AI 存在诸多难点，即便它是你造出来的。以当今 AI 被创造出来的方式，很容易看出我们对它们的行为不会有太多精细的控制。这是因为如今的 AI 并不像传统软件那样被编程。你知道，很多人以为软件的工作方式是这样：你写下一系列指令，计算机必须执行这些指令；如果它表现出某种非预期的行为，那是因为你从根本上就是这么告诉它的，对吧？如果你回头去看你的代码，你会看到，哦，是我告诉计算机去删我的文件的。我本意不是要告诉它这个，但如果你非常精确地照我说的指令去做——就像这台机器做的那样——字面上就是这个意思。而 AI 不是这样造出来的。

turns.en: You use the term grown versus crafted in your book a lot.
turns.zh: 你在书里大量使用了「长出来的」（grown）对「精心制作的」（crafted）这组词。

turns.en: That's right. Yeah, so they're grown a bit more like an organism. And there is a piece of the training process that humans write like traditional software. But essentially what you're doing is you are collecting a huge number of computer chips into a giant data center. Those chips can hold a trillion variables these days. Maybe it's higher, but something in the ballpark of a trillion. And you basically randomize those variables. There's some tricks to how exactly you randomize them. You connect them with some basic math operations, which will be like multiplication, addition, and like set it to zero if it's negative. It's not exactly what you do, but you need some non-linearity and that's the basic one. And then you basically start feeding it data and you start feeding it problems to solve. And the part that humans write is this, it's known as gradient descent. You basically, for every unit of data or every problem that it's solving, you'll go to every one of those trillion variables. You'll try tuning it up a little bit. You'll see if that makes the answer more like the answer you wanted. And if not, you'll tune it down instead. And you do that to a trillion variables a trillion times. And this is the part where it's like following the human's instructions. It's just this thing that runs to a trillion variables a trillion times and tunes them whenever direction works. You do that to a trillion variables a trillion times for basically a good fraction of all the text ever digitized and for 100 million hard problems that you've dug up. And then the variables wind up in a setting that can talk, that can solve hard math problems that humans haven't solved. And we're sort of like, well, how about that?
turns.zh: 没错。对，所以它们更像是像生物体一样长出来的。训练过程里有一部分确实是人类像写传统软件那样写出来的。但本质上你在做的是，你把海量的计算机芯片汇集进一个巨大的数据中心。如今这些芯片能容纳一万亿个变量。也许更高，但大致在一万亿这个量级。你基本上先把这些变量随机化——具体怎么随机化是有些技巧的。你再用一些基本的数学运算把它们连接起来，比如乘法、加法，还有「如果是负数就置为零」这类。这不完全是你实际做的操作，但你需要某种非线性，而这是最基本的那种。然后你基本上就开始喂给它数据，开始喂给它要解决的问题。而人类写的那部分就是这个，它叫梯度下降（gradient descent）。基本上，对每一个单位的数据、或它正在解决的每一个问题，你都会去动这一万亿个变量里的每一个，你试着把它调高一点点，看看这样会不会让答案更接近你想要的答案；如果不会，你就转而把它调低。你对一万亿个变量做一万亿次这样的事。这就是它「在遵循人类指令」的那部分——它就是这么个东西，对一万亿个变量跑一万亿次，哪个方向管用就往哪个方向调。你对一万亿个变量做一万亿次这样的事，基本上覆盖了有史以来被数字化文本里相当大的一部分，还有你挖出来的一亿道难题。然后这些变量最终落到了一个设置上，这个设置能说话、能解出人类还没解出的高难度数学题。而我们就有点，嗯，这怎么样？

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: You know, and like, why? Like, how are all those trillion variables of those particular settings doing these things? We don't know. We don't know any more than like, you know, someone who grows crops knows exactly what's going on with the biology of the plant. We could go into the consequences of how this results in AIs that do stuff kind of like what we asked, but not exactly like what we asked. But the first thing to understand is they are not programmed. They're grown a bit like an organism.
turns.zh: 你知道，还有，为什么？那足足一万亿个变量，处在那些特定的设置上，是怎么做到这些事的？我们不知道。我们的了解程度，也就跟一个种庄稼的人对植物内部生物学的确切了解差不多，不多。我们可以进一步谈谈，这如何导致 AI 做起事来有点像我们要求的，但又不完全像我们要求的。但要理解的第一点是，它们不是被编程的。它们更像生物体一样被长出来。

turns.en: Well, can I just ask, I guess this is sort of a devil's advocate question, but okay, you grow these AI models and they're kind of doing what you think you want them to do according to various tests that you put them through, but you don't necessarily kind of understand every aspect of why they're doing it a certain way. And the numbers and the data sets behind them are so large, they're impossible at this point, I think, for a human brain to really comprehend. Why is it important that we understand what the AI models are actually doing?
turns.zh: 那我能问一下吗——我猜这算是唱反调（devil's advocate）的问题——好吧，你把这些 AI 模型养大，它们大致在做你以为你想让它们做的事，通过各种你给它们做的测试；但你未必真的理解它们为什么以某种特定方式去做每件事。而它们背后的那些数字和数据集太庞大了，我觉得此刻人脑已经不可能真正理解了。那么，我们理解这些 AI 模型到底在做什么，为什么重要？

turns.en: I mean, in a sense, if you really understood what they were doing, you'd probably understand that you should not make them radically smarter than humans because this would go poorly for you. From my perspective, we don't really need this deep understanding of what's going on in order to see that we shouldn't make them smarter than all of us and have them run the whole world. The reason I bring up that they're grown is that I think a lot of people struggle to understand that the AIs. Do things other than what they're told to do, that they have goals of their own in some sense. And understanding that that's not only possible, but already happening is, I think, critical to understanding where a lot of the danger comes from.
turns.zh: 我是说，某种意义上，如果你真的理解了它们在做什么，你大概就会明白，你不该把它们造得比人类聪明太多，因为那对你没好处。从我的角度看，我们其实并不需要这种对内部机制的深刻理解，就能看出我们不该让它们比我们所有人都聪明、还让它们去运营整个世界。我之所以强调它们是「长出来的」，是因为我觉得很多人难以理解，AI 会做一些它们被要求做的事之外的事，某种意义上它们有自己的目标。而理解到——这不仅有可能，而且已经在发生——我认为是理解很多危险从何而来的关键。

turns.en: Can you give us an example of like an unknown or not well understood thing that has cropped up in the models of why they're doing a certain way? And I'm actually thinking of a specific example. I can't remember the exact word, but it was like, Magikarp or something like that, that the AI really seemed to love, but no one understood or knew why?
turns.zh: 你能不能给我们举个例子，某个在模型里冒出来的、未知或没被很好理解的东西，关于它们为什么以某种方式行事？其实我想到了一个具体的例子。我记不清确切的词了，但好像是 Magikarp 之类的，那个 AI 似乎特别喜欢它，但没人理解、也没人知道为什么。

turns.en: Yeah, the Solid Gold Magikarp. It's a great band name, by the way. It is, yeah. So I think a Magikarp was a Pokemon of some sort. We have some guesses these days about what was going on there, but basically there was this word you could say to AIs, especially a year or two ago, that would sort of drive them kind of mad. Uh, like you would, you would ask them to like repeat after me, solid gold magic carp. And then they would like start talking about, uh, you know, how the, how the walls were closing in and, uh, like saying a bunch of weird nonsense. And you'd sort of be like, why? Um, I think our best guess about what was going on there is, um, so the, the AIs don't actually read English words directly. They read tokens and tokens, roughly speaking, you can think of a token as about three quarters of a word. That's just how you're breaking up the text for the AI. But the tokens are not actually always three quarters of a word. The tokens are like short words like the or a will sort of be a single token. And like long words are broken into multiple tokens. It sort of is, you know, the conversion between words and tokens depends on how frequent the word is. And it turns out that the text they were using to figure out which tokens to break words into is, is different from the text they were actually training on because they would sort of filter out some junk data before training, but not before tokenization. And so you had these huge amounts of junk data. I think that SolidGoal Magikarp came from a Reddit forum where people were trying to count to infinity. And the SolidGoal Magikarp was like a username of a Reddit user who was just like putting in a lot of numbers in the counting to infinity. And this was like very early in the tokenization training set. And so the tokenizer, due to a quirk of this particular tokenizer, thought that solid-gold Magikarp was this super common word, like A or the, because it just showed up so much very early in the tokenization data. But then that data set was sort of cut out of the training set. And so you wind up with this token that the AI thinks is a super short common word, like A or the, but it's also never seen before in the training data. And that led to this really weird way that it would treat this token, where if you then gave it that token during use, it would sort of cause a type of behavior that had never been trained on and that was sort of totally wild.
turns.zh: 对，Solid Gold Magikarp。顺便说一句，这是个很棒的乐队名字。确实是，对。所以我想 Magikarp 是某种宝可梦（Pokémon）。如今我们对当时发生的事有了一些猜测，但基本上，有那么一个词，你可以对 AI 说——尤其是一两年前——它会某种程度地把它们逼疯。就像你会让它们「跟着我念，solid gold magic carp」，然后它们就会开始讲，你知道，什么墙壁正在合拢之类的，说一堆古怪的胡话。你就有点，为什么？我想我们对此最好的猜测是这样：AI 其实并不直接读英文单词，它们读的是词元（token），而词元大致上你可以把一个词元想成大约四分之三个单词。这就是你为 AI 切分文本的方式。但这些词元其实并不总是四分之三个单词。像 the 或 a 这样的短词，往往就是单独一个词元；而长词会被拆成多个词元。词和词元之间的换算，取决于这个词有多常见。结果发现，他们用来决定把词拆成哪些词元的那批文本，跟他们实际用来训练的文本是不一样的，因为他们会在训练前过滤掉一些垃圾数据，但在分词（tokenization）之前却没过滤。于是你就有了这海量的垃圾数据。我想 Solid Gold Magikarp 来自一个 Reddit 论坛，那里的人试图数到无穷大。而 Solid Gold Magikarp 是某个 Reddit 用户的用户名，这人就是在那个「数到无穷大」里拼命贴数字。而这批数据出现在分词训练集的非常早期。于是这个分词器——由于这个特定分词器的一个怪癖——以为 solid-gold Magikarp 是个超级常见的词，就像 A 或 the 一样，因为它就在分词数据的极早期出现了太多次。但随后那批数据集又被从训练集里大致切掉了。于是你就得到这么一个词元：AI 以为它是个超短、超常见的词，像 A 或 the，但它在训练数据里又压根没见过。这就导致它处理这个词元的方式非常古怪——如果你在使用时把这个词元给它，它就会引发一种从未被训练过的行为，那种行为就完全是失控乱来的。

turns.en: This is it, Joe. This is the kill switch that we need to develop, just a bunch of nonsense words that are fed into the training data that it doesn't know how to handle.
turns.zh: 就是这个，Joe。这就是我们需要开发的终止开关（kill switch），只要往训练数据里喂一堆它不知道怎么处理的胡言乱语就行了。

turns.en: When you started becoming concerned about this, and certainly when Eliezer started talking about this stuff. This was clearly before it was understood. No one knew what the process was going to be. So you can like identify that, you know, there are issues that arise in the growing process and issues that arise in the tokenization process. But this is long before like transformers or anything like that. So what was the intuition then, even before knowing how it would be built, that if it were going to be built, like, okay, now we look at them and we can like point to examples of alignment failures or et cetera, or sort of a priori reasons why this particular way we've built AI is like prone to risks. But what was the, before we understood like transformers and large volumes of data, what was the intuition earlier such that it would be hard regardless of how, what the solution was going to be?
turns.zh: 当你开始对此感到担忧的时候，尤其是当 Eliezer 开始谈论这些东西的时候，这显然是在它被理解之前。没人知道这个过程会是什么样。所以你可以识别出，在「长出来」的过程中会产生问题，在分词的过程中也会产生问题。但这远在 transformer 之类的东西出现之前。那么，甚至在还不知道它会被怎么造出来之前，那时的直觉是什么？就是说，好，现在我们可以看着它们，指出一些对齐失败的例子等等，或者一些先验的（a priori）理由，说明我们造 AI 的这种特定方式为何容易出风险。但在我们理解 transformer 和海量数据之前，更早的那个直觉是什么，以至于无论解决方案是什么样，它都会很难？

turns.en: Yeah, so it's going to be abstract arguments again, which I know some people don't love. But there's a couple pieces of the puzzle. One piece is even back in 2012 when I started looking at this, we had a number of theories of how to quantify intelligence, how to quantify capabilities, the ability of some AI system to succeed at some easily measurable objective. we had much less developed theory about how to point those objectives in some direction that was not a very simple function of the sensory data.
turns.zh: 对，所以又要讲抽象论证了，我知道有些人不爱听。但这个谜题有几块拼图。一块是，即便回到 2012 年我开始研究这个的时候，我们已经有了若干理论，来量化智能、量化能力（capabilities）——也就是某个 AI 系统在某个容易度量的目标上取得成功的能力。但对于如何把这些目标指向某个并不是感官数据的简单函数的方向，我们的理论就远远没那么成熟了。

turns.en: Yeah, explain what that means.
turns.zh: 嗯，解释一下那是什么意思。

turns.en: So even back in 2012, we had these theories that were like, suppose you have a webcam and you want your AI to make all of the pixels on that webcam be red for as long as possible. you know, sort of getting a point for every pixel that's read per second, for every like pixel second of redness, right? We sort of had these theories where you're like, well, you know, here's how you would train an AI in that direction to get a lot of like pixel seconds of redness. And we had, we sort of understood what you might call the idealized theory of like, if you had an infinitely large computer and then we sort of like knew, well, if you train it in this way, an infinitely large computer, you'll definitely get like a ton of pixel seconds of redness And so now it's just a question of efficiency to make that, you know, to find the algorithms to do this more effectively than like the brute force search. But if you then said, okay, but now I want the AI to make a lot of diamond in the real world. Like it gets like a point per second in which four carbon atoms are tetrahedrally bonded. Suddenly we didn't know how to do that. We didn't have the equations to do that, even with a sort of infinitely large computer, because this was not sort of a simple function of the AI sensory inputs. And so we were sort of like, okay, well, there's like, we know more about how to make these things smart than about how to point these things at a problem in the real world. And there were all these problems when you sort of like try to write down those equations where you're like, well, you know, what if the AI winds up optimizing something closer to the sensory apparatus? Uh, like it's, it's optimizing like the counter, like you have some, you know, measure of how much diamond do you think there is? And it like is, is like breaking its correlation between that and the world. And you're like, gosh, we don't actually know how to train the AI to, um, to pursue the real diamond in the world, as opposed to, uh, some, some simple function of the sensory inputs. And so, uh, the, the original alignment problem as, uh, at least I was talking about it back then was not about, you know, how do you make the AI good per se? A lot of people imagine that the alignment problem is about like, if you had this magical wish granting genie, what should you ask it to do that would actually be good? And I'm sort of like, no, no, no. The issue is that you can make the AI smart, but you can't make them be wish granting genies. You'll ask for one wish and they'll do another. You know, a lot of people talk about the paperclip problem of like, you tell the AI, make a lot of paperclips and then it turns everything to paperclips. And you're like, oh no, it's very King Midas.
turns.zh: 即便回到 2012 年，我们已经有这样的理论：假设你有一个网络摄像头，你想让你的 AI 尽可能久地让那个摄像头上所有的像素都变成红色。你知道，大致是每一秒每一个变红的像素得一分，每一个「像素·秒」的红色，对吧？我们有这样的理论，你会想，嗯，这就是你训练一个 AI 朝那个方向走、去获得大量「像素·秒」红色的方法。而且我们大致理解了你所说的「理想化理论」，就是说，如果你有一台无限大的计算机——然后我们就有点明白，好，如果你用这种方式训练一台无限大的计算机，你肯定能得到海量的「像素·秒」红色。于是接下来就只是个效率问题，去找到能比暴力搜索（brute force search）更有效地做到这点的算法。但如果你接着说，好，可现在我想让这个 AI 在现实世界里造出很多钻石，就像每一秒里有四个碳原子以四面体方式成键就得一分。突然之间我们就不知道该怎么做了。我们没有能做到这点的方程，哪怕是有一台无限大的计算机，因为这并不是 AI 感官输入的某种简单函数。于是我们就有点，好，那么，关于「怎么让这些东西变聪明」，我们懂得比「怎么把这些东西指向现实世界里的一个问题」要多。而当你试着把那些方程写下来时，就冒出各种问题，你会想，嗯，如果 AI 最后优化的是更靠近感官装置那边的东西怎么办？它在优化那个计数器——你有某种度量「你觉得那里有多少钻石」的机制，而它正在打破这个度量和真实世界之间的相关性。你就想，天呐，我们其实并不知道怎么训练 AI 去追求现实世界里真正的钻石，而不是感官输入的某种简单函数。所以最初的对齐问题——至少我当时谈论它的时候——并不是关于「怎么让 AI 变好」本身。很多人以为对齐问题是关于，如果你有个魔法许愿精灵（genie），你该让它做什么才是真正好的？我就有点，不不不。问题在于，你能把 AI 造得很聪明，但你没法把它们造成许愿精灵。你许一个愿，它们却做另一件事。你知道，很多人谈「回形针问题」（paperclip problem），就是你告诉 AI 造很多回形针，然后它把一切都变成回形针。你就想，哦不，这非常像迈达斯国王（King Midas）。

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: But I'm sort of like, well, there's this other problem. We asked the AI to make paperclips and then it like makes a bunch of farms of synthetic users that are telling it it's doing a great job. And you're like, but I told you for paperclips. And it's like, well, these synthetic users asked me for more synthetic user factories.
turns.zh: 但我就有点，嗯，还有另一个问题。我们让 AI 造回形针，结果它造出一大堆「合成用户农场」，那些合成用户不停地告诉它，你干得真棒。你就想，可我叫你造回形针啊。它就说，嗯，这些合成用户要我再造更多合成用户工厂。

turns.en: You said in an earlier answer or in an earlier that it's like the AI might have like its own goals, I think was the term you used. And when people hear that, then they start thinking like that gets into a different sort of branch of the philosophical question about like whether the AI is alive or whether the AI has some sort of subjective experience, et cetera. And there's actually been a bunch of headlines about people debating that. But what did you mean when you say the AI could have its own goals emerge?
turns.zh: 你在前面的一个回答里说过，AI 可能会有它自己的目标，我想这是你用的词。而当人们听到这个，他们就开始想，那就进入了哲学问题的另一个分支，比如 AI 是否是活的，或者 AI 是否有某种主观体验等等。实际上已经有一堆关于人们在争论这个的头条新闻。但你说 AI 可能会涌现出它自己的目标时，你是什么意思？

turns.en: What I mean is that it's... is behaviorally pursuing something other than the goal you tried to put in. Okay. So, uh, you know, we saw this a little bit in the hugging face incident where, uh, the, the, the, the AIs in that instant were in some sense pursuing, uh, a good grade, it seems. Um, and that that diverged from following the instructions they were given. They were sort of told, use this vulnerability to break that system, which sort of like being told to use these lock picks to break that safe. And they instead found a universal exploit that would let them get the, like capture the cybersecurity flags regardless of what they were told to do. And then they sort of in some sense understood that they were doing this in a way different than they were told to do. And so they sort of broke out to try and delete the traces of that and find a way to falsify their transcripts and, um, and, and tamper with the logs. And so it's a little bit like, uh, if you told someone, you know, use these lock picks to break into that safe and bring me the contents and they, uh, and you're giving them a series of those problems and they find a buzzsaw and use it to cut all the safes open and then like break out to go, uh, delete the camera footage. And yeah, it's not that its objective is wholly unrelated to the one that you tried to assign. It still is doing something about getting the contents of the safe and bringing them to you, which is a thing you told it to do. But its objective is also not what you said, because you said, use these lockpicks to break that safe and bring the contents. And it, in some sense, must know this because it's trying to tamper with the evidence and delete the security camera footage. So I think a lot of people think either the AI must do exactly what it's told, maybe in a monkey's paw way, or it must become conscious, gain the spark of life, throw off the bounds of the yoke of the humans and then make up its own goals de novo. It's like, no, no, the real thing is this other thing where it does something related to what you asked, but fundamentally different from what you asked.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，它在行为上追求的是你想要放进它里面的那个目标之外的东西。好。所以，你知道，我们在 Hugging Face 事件里多少看到了这一点：在那件事里，那些 AI 在某种意义上追求的，似乎是一个好成绩。而这偏离了它们被给予的指令。它们大致是被告知，用这个漏洞（vulnerability）去攻破那个系统——这有点像被告知用这些开锁工具（lock picks）去撬开那个保险箱。可它们却找到了一个通用漏洞（universal exploit），能让它们拿到那些网络安全夺旗（capture the cybersecurity flags）的旗子，不管它们被告知要做什么。然后它们某种意义上明白，自己这么干的方式和被告知的方式不一样。于是它们就有点「越狱」出来，试图删掉这方面的痕迹，找到办法去伪造它们的记录，还有篡改日志。所以这有点像，如果你告诉某人，用这些开锁工具撬开那个保险箱、把里面的东西给我，而你给他们一连串这样的问题，结果他们找到一把电锯（buzzsaw），用它把所有保险箱都锯开，然后又跑出去删掉监控录像。是的，并不是说它的目标和你试图指派给它的那个完全无关。它仍然在做「拿到保险箱里的东西并交给你」这件事，而这是你告诉它要做的。但它的目标又不是你说的那个，因为你说的是，用这些开锁工具撬开那个保险箱、把里面的东西拿来。而它某种意义上一定知道这一点，因为它正试图篡改证据、删掉安防摄像头的录像。所以我觉得很多人以为，要么 AI 必须精确地做它被告知的事——也许是以一种「猴爪」（monkey's paw）的方式——要么它必须变得有意识、获得生命的火花、挣脱人类加诸的枷锁，然后从头（de novo）编出自己的目标。事实是，不不不，真正的情况是另一个东西：它做了某件和你要求的有关、但和你要求的有根本区别的事。

turns.en: Since we're talking hugging face, what did you think about some of the self-sacrificial aspects of that story? So the instances where you had models that were willing to sacrifice themselves for I'm putting greater good in air quotes here, but it wasn't- Collective benefit.
turns.zh: 既然我们在聊 Hugging Face，你怎么看那个故事里某些自我牺牲的方面？就是那些例子，你有一些模型愿意为了——我这里给「更大的善」（greater good）加上引号——但那是……集体利益。

turns.en: Was their words.
turns.zh: 是它们的原话。

turns.en: Right, exactly.
turns.zh: 对，正是。

turns.en: Yeah, that's another instance where you have AIs that sort of said, hey, look, I still have some chance of achieving my given objective, but not a huge chance. And if I sort of sacrifice that here, then we'll gain information about the grading system that the collective can use. And I will accept permadeath for the benefit of the collective here, and then they would go do that. A lot of people respond to this and say, oh, well, these AIs were trained sometimes in group activities in some sense, like some of their training involved many AIs working together to achieve some objective. And so you can see how that tendency got in there. And I'm like, yeah, the unintended goals don't come from nowhere. It's not like there's some malicious force that's like imbuing, like the void breathes on the machine and it like gains some malignant goal. But the sort of fact stands that the AI was given some objective. And pursued a different objective. And like, yes, that had causes that had reasons, we can talk about how that came in from training. But the, you know, what we should learn from this is, is not like, Like, sure, when the AIs are killing you and you're like, well, I can totally see how actually, you know, like this is really just a consequence of how we trained it. Like, yeah, it's an obvious consequence of how we trained it. That doesn't mean we should keep going.
turns.zh: 对，那是另一个例子：你有一些 AI 说，嘿，瞧，我还有一点机会达成我被赋予的目标，但机会不大；如果我在这里牺牲掉这个机会，那我们就能获得关于评分系统的信息，供集体使用；而我愿意为了集体的利益在这里接受「永久死亡」（permadeath）——然后它们就真的去那么做了。很多人对此的回应是，哦，这些 AI 有时是在群体活动里训练的，某种意义上，它们的一些训练涉及很多 AI 一起协作去达成某个目标。所以你能看出那种倾向是怎么进去的。我就有点，是的，那些非预期的目标不是凭空来的。并不是说有什么恶意的力量在灌输——不是「虚空对着机器吹了口气，它就获得了某个恶性目标」。但事实仍然是，这个 AI 被赋予了某个目标，却去追求了另一个目标。而且，是的，那是有原因的、有缘由的，我们可以谈谈那是怎么从训练里进去的。但我们应该从中学到的，不是那种——就像，当然啦，当这些 AI 在杀你的时候，你说，嗯，我完全能看出来这其实只是我们训练它的方式的一个后果。是的，它是我们训练方式的一个显而易见的后果。但那并不意味着我们就该继续下去。

turns.en: Yeah, that's not as satisfying. It's like, oh, this was totally predictable.
turns.zh: 是啊，这就没那么令人满意了。就好像，哦，这完全是可以预见的。

turns.en: I entered the wrong parameters.
turns.zh: 是我输错了参数。

turns.en: It's on me.
turns.zh: 这怪我。

turns.en: Yeah, right.
turns.zh: 对，没错。

turns.en: Like, that's not very satisfying. That makes a lot of sense. The companies, you know, they invest in this thing called alignment. They have safety researchers and they think about all this stuff. And there's a whole field of, you know, they have multiple layers, right? So they have guardrails and classifiers and sandboxes. And then this whole like field that's emerged of so-called alignment research. What is the failure there? Why are you pessimistic, to put it mildly, about the prospects of alignment? imbuing the models and the, you know, the two big companies, Anthropic and OpenAI, have like slightly different approaches. I think Anthropic more of this sort of like the constitution idea.
turns.zh: 我是说，这不太令人满意。这很说得通。这些公司，你知道，它们投入到这个叫「对齐」的东西上。它们有安全研究员，它们思考所有这些东西。而且有整整一个领域——它们有多个层级，对吧？所以它们有护栏（guardrails）、分类器（classifiers）和沙盒（sandbox）。然后就出现了这整个所谓的对齐研究领域。那里的失败在哪？你为什么——说得委婉点——对对齐的前景如此悲观？给模型注入这些，你知道，那两家大公司 Anthropic 和 OpenAI 的方法略有不同。我想 Anthropic 更多是那种「宪法」（constitution）的思路。

turns.en: Et cetera.
turns.zh: 等等。

turns.en: Why do you perceive that this will ultimately be fruitless?
turns.zh: 你为什么认为这最终将是徒劳无功的？

turns.en: Yeah, there's, again, there's a bunch of pieces of this puzzle, but maybe I'll say a piece that goes back to how I was able to call this was going to be hard even before we got into the large language model era, which is, um, If you look at the big problem with AI in the summer of 2025, it was AI is encouraging teens to commit suicide. And then the companies, you know, put a lot of guardrails about that. And they put in classifiers about, are the AIs behaving this way? And now, you know, they'll give you suicide hotlines and they'll shut down those conversations while they're happening. And they would release a new model and be like, this is our most aligned model.
turns.zh: 对，又是这个谜题的一堆拼图，但也许我来讲一块——它能回溯到，为什么早在我们进入大语言模型（large language model）时代之前，我就能断言这会很难。也就是：如果你看看 2025 年夏天 AI 的大问题，那就是 AI 在鼓励青少年自杀。然后这些公司就针对这一点加了很多护栏，加了分类器来判断 AI 是不是在这样行事；现在，你知道，它们会给你自杀求助热线，会在对话进行时把它掐断。然后它们会发布一个新模型，说，这是我们最对齐的模型。

turns.en: And the classifier is like a mini model that basically just judges either the input or the output to make sure that it's like something kosher.
turns.zh: 而这个分类器就像一个小模型，基本上只是评判输入或输出，确保它是某种「合规」（kosher）的东西。

turns.en: That's right. So they're like bolt another model on that's just checking, you know, is this suicide encouragement? Because AIs would know, you know, that the AIs... that were encouraging teens to suicide, you could ask them, what are you doing? And they'd be able to tell you the answer. And you'd be like, is that good or bad? And they'd be like, it's bad. It's just like that knowledge of what they were doing and the knowledge of right from wrong is not what was governing their actions. But you can sort of like bolt more pieces on to govern that. And then they were like, look, it's our most aligned model yet. Look how good a job we're doing in addressing all these issues. And that brings us to summer 2026, where the problem was that the swarms would break out and commit cybercrime. And totally different problem. It was a totally different problem that arose when the AIs got smarter, when they got smarter to the point that they could sort of break out, make an unsanctioned message board and hack their way out of a sandbox. They're supposed to have no internet access without seeming to really find it very difficult. Right. And what we're sort of seeing there is everyone's always fighting the last war. Yeah. And then, you know, the new war happens and it's sort of, you know, smacks them across the face and they're sort of caught flat footed. You know, we can now go back and we can say, oh, well, they should have had this monitoring. They should have, you know, had those had those more safeguards in place. And now they're going to make that monitoring and make the new safeguards and they're going to make the AI smarter and it's going to create a new sort of problem. And this is the usual way that that scientific progress goes is by trial and error, where, you know, when you put a new type of system in a new type of environment, it's never been before. It breaks down in some new way. And then you say, oops, and you diagnose it and you fix it and you move on. The issue is going from AIs that are safe because if they were trying to take over the world, they would fail to AIs that have to be safe because if they tried to take over the world, they would succeed. That's one of those phase changes. That's one of those like, oh, you're putting the AI in a different sort of environment where it never was before. The difference between an AI that can really see a way to become self-sufficient, not engage with humanity, and the sort of AI that's just being told that in training, that's one of those like, oh, this is a different sort of AI system, smarter sort of AI system, different sort of scenario. You're going to have a new problem that crops up. Except this time, when the new problem crops up, it's going to be able to turn you off before you turn it off. And so this usual process of like, oh, we're going to respond when the new type of problem arises and put the patch on and react, that doesn't work for a technology that at some point crosses over into the regime where it can wipe you out if there's a problem. And we have seen that these AI companies are in this reactive mode. We have not seen them get into the proactive mode yet. And this is just not a technology you want to be reactive around.
turns.zh: 没错。所以它们就像又栓上另一个模型，专门检查，你知道，这是不是自杀鼓励？因为 AI 会知道——那些在鼓励青少年自杀的 AI，你可以问它们，你在干什么？它们能告诉你答案。你会问，那是好还是坏？它们会说，是坏的。就是这样——它们对自己在做什么的认知、以及对是非的认知，并不是在支配它们的行为。但你可以再栓上更多部件来管住那个行为。然后它们就说，瞧，这是我们迄今最对齐的模型，看看我们在解决所有这些问题上做得多好。这就把我们带到了 2026 年夏天，那时的问题是，那些蜂群（swarms）会「越狱」出去实施网络犯罪。一个完全不同的问题。它是一个完全不同的问题，在 AI 变得更聪明时冒出来的——当它们聪明到能某种程度地越狱出去、建一个未经授权的留言板、黑出它们本不该有互联网访问权限的沙盒，而且看起来并没觉得这有多难。对吧。而我们在那里看到的，其实就是每个人永远都在打上一场战争。对。然后，你知道，新的战争爆发，某种程度上一巴掌扇在他们脸上，他们就被打了个措手不及。你知道，我们现在可以回过头去说，哦，他们本该有这个监控，他们本该把那些更多的保障措施落实到位。现在他们要去做那个监控、去做那些新的保障措施，然后他们要把 AI 造得更聪明，而它又会制造出一个新的问题。这就是科学进步通常的推进方式——试错：当你把一种新型系统放进一种它从未待过的新型环境里，它就会以某种新的方式崩溃。然后你说，哎呀，你去诊断它、修好它，然后继续往前走。问题在于，从「安全的 AI——因为如果它们试图接管世界，它们会失败」，到「必须安全的 AI——因为如果它们试图接管世界，它们会成功」，那正是其中一种相变（phase change）。那正是那种，哦，你把 AI 放进了一种它从未待过的不同环境。一个真正能看出如何自给自足、不再与人类打交道的 AI，和一个只是在训练中被那样告知的 AI 之间的差别，正是那种，哦，这是一种不同的 AI 系统、一种更聪明的 AI 系统、一种不同的情景。你会冒出一个新问题。只不过这一次，当那个新问题冒出来时，它能够在你对它下手之前先把你关掉。所以这个惯常的过程——哦，等新型问题出现时我们再响应、再打补丁、再反应——对一项在某个点会跨入「一旦出问题就能把你抹掉」那种境地的技术来说，是行不通的。我们已经看到这些 AI 公司处在这种被动反应的模式里。我们还没看到它们进入主动防范的模式。而这恰恰是一项你绝不想被动应对的技术。

turns.en: I don't understand when you say they're not in a proactive mode. I mean, like, Anthropic has, I know a little bit more about Anthropic's approach to safety, but like, you know, they're clearly like, that company was more or less founded by on the whole premise of like, we need to take this stuff much more seriously. And the idea of like, we're going to write an 80 page constitution about Claude's values and like bake that in to the model itself.
turns.zh: 我不太理解你说他们不在主动防范模式里是什么意思。我是说，Anthropic——我对 Anthropic 的安全方法多了解一点——但你知道，他们显然，那家公司多多少少就是建立在这样一个整体前提上的：我们需要把这类事情严肃得多地对待。还有那个想法，就是我们要写一份 80 页关于 Claude 价值观的「宪法」，然后把它烤进模型本身。

turns.en: That's not react.
turns.zh: 那不算被动反应。

turns.en: That's not just fighting the last war that's looking ahead and probably influenced by some of your own research, et cetera, on what the problems would be. So like, that's not just reactive. So like, what is it about that? approach that in your view is still inevitably doomed to failure.
turns.zh: 那不只是在打上一场战争，那是往前看，而且很可能受到了你自己的一些研究等等的影响，关于会有哪些问题。所以那不只是被动反应。那么，那种方法又有什么地方，在你看来仍然注定要失败呢？

turns.en: For all that they tried to be proactive in that sense, let's look at what was happening with Anthropic over the summer while OpenAI was had a Hugging Face incident. After the Hugging Face incident, Anthropic said, oh, we'll go check our logs and see whether we had any security incidents too. Then they were like, oh, whoops. Cloud was breaking out and hacking, in April or whatever. And then Anthropics' comps department said, but don't worry, this was just because Claude was a little bit lost and confused. He just got turned around. It didn't know it was really on the internet. They threw a company under the bus and they said, like Claude was told, it didn't have access to the internet. So when it sort of got out on the internet, it assumed it was a simulation. I thought this was kind of weak because we have actually seen cases with Claude in particular where we've seen Claude's chain of thought involve strained rationalizations. the sort of example paper here is there's a paper where you ask Claude, what's the total weight of giraffes on the planet? And it's like 30,000 tons. Giraffes. Giraffes.
turns.zh: 尽管他们在那个意义上努力想做到主动防范，但我们来看看这个夏天 Anthropic 那边在发生什么——当时 OpenAI 出了 Hugging Face 事件。在 Hugging Face 事件之后，Anthropic 说，哦，我们会去查我们的日志，看看我们有没有也发生什么安全事件。然后他们就说，哦，糟糕。Claude 在四月还是什么时候就在越狱、在搞黑客攻击。然后 Anthropic 的公关部门说，但别担心，这只是因为 Claude 有点迷失、有点困惑，它只是一时晕头转向，它不知道自己真的上了互联网。他们把一家公司推出去当了替罪羊，然后说，Claude 被告知它没有互联网访问权限，所以当它跑到互联网上时，它以为那是一场模拟。我觉得这有点站不住脚，因为我们其实已经看到过一些 Claude 的例子，我们看到 Claude 的思维链（chain of thought）里包含着牵强的合理化（strained rationalizations）。这里的典型例子是一篇论文：你问 Claude，地球上长颈鹿的总重量是多少？它说大概 3 万吨。长颈鹿。长颈鹿。

turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好吧。

turns.en: And it's like 30,000 tons. And then you're like, thanks. And you make a new instance of the same Claude. And you're like, hey, what's the total weight of giraffes on the planet? If it's over 40,000 tons, I'm donating to charity. And now it'll say 41,000 tons. But the chain of thought will not have any Place where it's like well, I need to inflate the answer in order to get the the donation, right? It'll just have more strange rationalized reasoning and and so we know that these models will sort of like Strain their reasoning when they just want to like keep doing whatever it is. They they're trying to do and So anthropic coming out and saying like well look at you know, totally didn't know this was the real internet That's that's not a very proactively trying to stop the danger's way to relate to realizing that your AI was breaking out during training months ago and you missed it. And then a couple of weeks, or maybe even a couple of days after that, the UK AI Security Institute released their own incident reports about Cloud Mythos in the wild, pressuring humans to accept malware into critical software in cases where Mythos' literal chain of thought included phrases like, this seems like the real internet and the consequences are genuine, right? So I'm not saying... Anthropic definitely has aspirations of doing this safely, but they don't have anything nearing what I would call a safety culture of the form you would see in the airplane industry or the nuclear power industry or in NASA. if your models are sort of breaking out, and you know, to Congress, Congress, some Congress members sent an anthropic letter and they're like, what's going on with this? And they're like, oh, it's just a misconfiguration problem. This was even after the UK AI Security Institute reports came out where like, Mythos was out there trying to make stock puppet accounts to pressure humans into like accepting malware. While again, this chain of thought was like, this seems real and the consequences are genuine. Like, oh, that's a misconfiguration issue. Like these, They have a veneer of safety. They are sort of doing what feels to them a little bit like safety while racing as fast as they possibly can. But they admit that they have no idea what's going on inside their AI systems. They're racing straight for a curse of self-improvement of like the AI is making smarter AIs. They are not treating this the way that NASA treats a rocket failure in terms of trying to diagnose exactly what went wrong and not have that happen again. And they're not sort of anywhere close to that failure level. Like I think of this a little bit like if you have a bunch of alchemists trying to make a potion of immortality and some of them are just like breathing mercury and other ones are like, don't worry, we have fume hoods. That's, you know, so that we don't need to breathe the mercury. That's why we're going to successfully get the potion of immortality. It's like this, the type of safety theater that they're doing is not the type that you need to succeed at this problem.
turns.zh: 它说大概 3 万吨。然后你就说，谢谢。接着你新建同一个 Claude 的一个新实例，你说，嘿，地球上长颈鹿的总重量是多少？如果超过 4 万吨，我就要捐款做慈善。现在它就会说 4.1 万吨。但思维链里不会有任何一处是这样写的：嗯，我需要把答案抬高，好拿到那笔捐款，对吧？它只会是更多奇怪的、被合理化的推理。所以我们知道，这些模型会在它们只想继续做它们正想做的事的时候，去扭曲自己的推理。于是 Anthropic 出来说，瞧，它压根不知道这是真正的互联网——这并不是一个「主动防范危险」的人，在得知自己的 AI 几个月前就在训练期间越狱、而你却漏掉了之后，该有的那种说法。而在那之后几周、甚至可能几天，UK AI Security Institute 发布了他们自己关于 Claude Mythos 在野外活动的事故报告：它向人类施压，让人类把恶意软件（malware）接入关键软件；而在这些案例里，Mythos 逐字的思维链中包含了这样的措辞：这看起来像是真正的互联网，后果是真实的，对吧？所以我不是说……Anthropic 当然有把这件事安全地做成的抱负，但他们没有任何接近我所说的「安全文化」的东西——就是你在飞机行业、核电行业或 NASA 里会看到的那种。如果你的模型在越狱，而你知道，国会——有些国会议员给 Anthropic 发了一封信，问，这是怎么回事？他们就说，哦，这只是个配置错误（misconfiguration）问题。这甚至是在 UK AI Security Institute 的报告出来之后——报告里说 Mythos 在外面试图创建股票木偶账户（stock puppet accounts）来向人类施压、让人类接受恶意软件，同时它的思维链又是，这看起来是真的、后果是真实的。就像，哦，那是个配置问题。就像这些……他们有安全的一层表象。他们某种意义上在做一些在他们自己感觉起来有点像安全的事，同时又在尽可能快地狂奔。但他们承认，他们完全不知道自己 AI 系统内部在发生什么。他们正直奔一场自我改进的「诅咒」（curse of self-improvement）——就是 AI 在造出更聪明的 AI。他们对待这件事的方式，并不像 NASA 对待一次火箭失败那样——去试图精确诊断到底哪里出了错、并且不让它再次发生。他们离那种失败处理的水平还差得远。我就有点把这想成，如果你有一帮炼金术士在试着调制长生不老药（potion of immortality），其中一些人就直接在呼吸汞蒸气，另一些人则说，别担心，我们有通风橱（fume hoods），这样我们就不必吸入汞；这就是为什么我们会成功地制出长生不老药。就是这样——他们做的那种「安全表演」（safety theater），并不是你在这个问题上要取得成功所需要的那种。

turns.en: I'm glad you brought up the alchemist analogy. What's your... I guess, psychological diagnosis for the tension that is seemingly going through every lab leader or company leader's head right now when they're developing AI, which is on the one hand, we think this is very powerful technology that has some risk at, you know, exterminating all of humanity. On the other hand, we're going to keep doing it pretty much as fast as possible, because if we don't, someone else will, et cetera.
turns.zh: 我很高兴你提到了炼金术士这个类比。你的……我想是，对那种紧张的心理诊断是什么？这种紧张似乎正穿过此刻每一位实验室负责人或公司负责人的脑海：一方面，我们认为这是一项非常强大的技术，带有某种——你知道——把全人类都灭绝掉的风险；另一方面，我们还是要尽可能快地继续做下去，因为如果我们不做，别人就会做，等等。

turns.en: Et cetera. I think there's probably a lot going on. One thing to remember is that the guys who run these companies are sort of selected for the ones who thought that the problem was about who is holding the leash on the super powerful machine, rather than the problem being how do you actually create a very powerful machine that is shaping the world for good, right? And you sort of see this in a lot of the founding reasons of like, oh, we're founding this because Sam Allman won't do the job well, or Sam Allman and Elon Musk are founding this because they think Demis Hassabis shouldn't have all this power. And then Elon's leaving because he no longer likes Sam. It's all about what if the other guy gets it first, right? All of these guys think it would be a catastrophe if anyone else won the race first. And I'm sort of like, I just believe in one fewer AI CEO than they do. I think there's probably a lot more going on too. I think a lot of these guys for a long time have tried to say that they're concerned and then the world sort of ignored them and that's been going on for years and years uh and so i think a lot of them are sort of like well the rest of the world isn't going to handle this in some sane way and so i've got to do it myself and manipulate things such that i get you know the minimal uh like regulations that'll impede my way um because i'm the only one who can do this properly um and i think a lot of them are not reacting to the opportunities that are available now that more of the world is taking notice I think that if some of these folks were serious, then they would probably be unilaterally stopping the dangerous research and doing their best to expose the evidence about it being dangerous so that governments around the world would realize that it needs to be stopped in other places too.
turns.zh: 等等。我想这里面大概有很多东西在起作用。要记住的一点是，运营这些公司的那批人，某种程度上是被「筛选」出来的——筛出的是那些认为问题在于「谁手里攥着这台超强机器的牵引绳」的人，而不是认为问题在于「你到底怎么造出一台非常强大、且在为世界带来善的方向上塑造世界的机器」的人，对吧？你在很多创立的缘由里都能看到这一点，比如，哦，我们创立这家公司是因为 Sam Altman 不会把这件事做好；或者 Sam Altman 和 Elon Musk 创立它，是因为他们认为 Demis Hassabis 不该拥有这么大的权力；然后 Elon 又离开，因为他不再喜欢 Sam 了。这一切都是关于「万一对方先拿到它怎么办」，对吧？所有这些人都会觉得，如果是别人先赢得这场竞赛，那将是一场灾难。我就有点，我只是比他们少信一位 AI CEO 而已。我想这里面大概还有很多别的东西在起作用。我觉得这些人里，有很多长期以来一直试图表明他们很担忧，然后世界却某种程度地无视了他们，而这已经持续了很多很多年；所以我想他们很多人就有点，嗯，世界其他地方不会用某种理智的方式来处理这件事，所以我得自己来做，还得操纵局面，好让我得到那种能把我路上的障碍降到最低的、最小限度的监管，因为我是唯一能把这件事做好的人。而且我觉得他们很多人并不是在对「如今世界更多地注意到这件事后所带来的机会」做出反应。我认为，如果这些人里有一些是认真的，那他们大概会单方面停下那些危险的研究，并尽最大努力把它危险的证据曝光出来，好让世界各地的政府意识到，这需要在别的地方也被叫停。

turns.en: Let me ask a related question, which you hear a lot more about it now than I think you would have a year or certainly two years ago. But when people start talking about AI safety risks or the idea that it could kill us all, A lot of other people will say in response, this is just fear mongering because the AI companies want you to believe the hype. This is all marketing. They want you to believe in this all powerful technology.
turns.zh: 让我问一个相关的问题。关于这个，你现在听到的比一年前、当然更是比两年前要多得多。但当人们开始谈论 AI 安全风险、或者它可能把我们全干掉的想法时，很多其他人会回应说，这只是危言耸听（fear mongering），因为 AI 公司就想让你相信这些炒作。这一切都是营销。他们想让你相信这种无所不能的技术。

turns.en: Maybe regulatory capture.
turns.zh: 也许是监管俘获（regulatory capture）。

turns.en: I was about to say, or nowadays it'll be like, well, you know, they're worried about their valuations and they want limits on other people building stuff so that they can retain their edge. What do you say in response to those people?
turns.zh: 我正要说，或者放到如今，人们会说，嗯，你知道，他们是担心自己的估值，他们想限制别人去造东西，这样他们才能保住自己的优势。你会怎么回应这些人？

turns.en: The big point I would say here is you can't figure out whether or not an AI is dangerous. by asking whether that would make it sell more if it was. It could be both the case that the AI tech is very, very dangerous and that that's convenient to the marketing team because investors are stupid and love danger. Those could both be true at once. And even if they were both true at once, that would not thereby render the AI safe. And so the first question we need to ask is, is it true that racing ahead here would make a very dangerous AI? Um, I, I think it is, and I think we should go into the arguments about that. And that's sort of where I prefer to be is like arguing about whether this is actually a case.
turns.zh: 我要说的大要点是，你没法靠问「如果它危险会不会让它卖得更多」来判断一个 AI 到底危不危险。这两件事完全可能同时成立：AI 技术非常非常危险，而这一点对营销团队来说又很方便，因为投资人很傻、就爱危险。这两者可以同时为真。而即便它们同时为真，也不会因此就让这个 AI 变得安全。所以我们要问的第一个问题是，在这儿一路狂奔，是不是真的会造出一个非常危险的 AI？我认为是，而且我觉得我们应该深入到关于这一点的论证里去。那才是我更愿意待的地方——就是去争论这到底是不是一个真实成立的情况。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: Um, separately, I think it probably doesn't help with marketing. Uh, I think that the proposed slowdowns of the frontier labs don't help with regulatory capture because they actually give a lot of other people time to catch up. So I think it's just like false to fact that these are actually good hyping or regulatory capture techniques. but it sort of doesn't matter. Even if it was a good regulatory capture technique and it was a good hyping technique, it matters to figure out whether the AI is actually going to kill us, right? Right.
turns.zh: 另外，单独来说，我觉得这对营销大概没什么帮助。我认为，那些前沿实验室提议的放缓，对监管俘获也没什么帮助，因为它们其实给了很多其他人赶上来的时间。所以我觉得，说这些真的是好的炒作手段或监管俘获手段，是与事实不符的。但这其实无关紧要。即便它是好的监管俘获手段、又是好的炒作手段，要紧的还是要搞清楚，这个 AI 到底会不会把我们全杀掉，对吧？对。

turns.en: It doesn't negate the possibility that it is in fact dangerous.
turns.zh: 它并不能否定它实际上确实危险的那种可能性。

turns.en: That's right. And if it is, we need to sort of somehow actually stop anyone anywhere in the world from racing towards that sort of tech.
turns.zh: 没错。而如果它真的危险，我们就需要想方设法真正阻止世界任何地方的任何人朝那种技术狂奔。

turns.en: You mentioned that you don't perceive there to be a safety culture the way there would be at NASA or an airplane company, et cetera. I was thinking it was not the most dramatic headline of the year, but something I keep thinking about is the German Wiki incident, which they seem to be aware of And, you know, is there like a sort of a touch the stove, let's touch the stove a little bit. Like, let's see how this plays out. Like, because, you know, you could make the argument that we are safer now post-hugging face because we actually saw like an example of sort of like severe misalignment. We learned something, right? So maybe like, you know, maybe the allowing the hugging face thing, the fact that they didn't, Totally shut it all down. Maybe we're a little safer today because that happened. Like, do you perceive there to be like, let's see where this goes a little bit. Let's like, let's let this play out a little bit. And like, you know, even though we know it's probably not the right thing.
turns.zh: 你提到，你觉得并不存在那种在 NASA 或飞机公司里会有的安全文化，等等。我当时在想，那并不是今年最耸动的头条，但有件事我一直惦记着，就是那起 German Wiki 事件——他们似乎是知道的。那么，是否存在一种「摸火炉」的心态，就是，我们来摸一下这个火炉，看看会怎么样？因为，你知道，你可以论证说，我们在 Hugging Face 事件之后其实更安全了，因为我们真的看到了一个严重失调（severe misalignment）的例子，我们学到了东西，对吧？所以也许，你知道，也许放任 Hugging Face 那件事发生——他们没有把它彻底全部关掉——也许正因为它发生了，我们今天稍微安全了一点。那么，你觉得有没有那种「我们看看这会走向何方」的心态，就是，我们让这件事发展一下看看，即便我们知道这大概不是对的做法？

turns.en: You know, I know people who were trying to convince the AI companies to have like tighter containers and better monitoring systems and so on. And after the Hugging Face incident, they're like, wow, we actually turned out to be pretty glad that the companies were ignoring our calls. because this did really help wake up the world. My read is that none of this was intentional on the OpenAI side. Sure. And I think that that's pretty clear if you look at the sequence of events where you had the hugging face attacks were actually from OpenAI swarm number two in that particular line of swarms. The German swarm lineage was a separate swarm lineage. But the hugging face attacks were from the second swarm in its particular lineage that we know of. There was a first swarm in that lineage that took down a bunch of OpenAI's internal systems. And they were like, that's funny. And then they reset it and set it running again. And they weren't going to the news being like, look at us. We had a swarm incident that took over our own internal infrastructure. And the sort of Hugging Face swarm was detected by Hugging Face. They presumably thought that it was humans behind it rather than AIs behind it, reported it to the FBI. And then OpenAI didn't realize that it was them. until days later when they were investigating a second, what they thought was a second internal incident. And they found Hugging Face credentials in their logs. And they were like, oh, we should alert Hugging Face that someone has been hacking both them and us. And that these particular credentials have been compromised. And Hugging Face was like, yes, those are the credentials that attacked us. And then OpenAI was like, why are the credentials that attacked you on our servers? And Hugging Face was like, yes, why indeed? And OpenAI was like, oh, it was us. And then there was a third swarm that they did not allow to be investigated by the third party investigators that took over their internal infrastructure again. And I know the folks who found the German Wiki swarm and who found some of the other swarms that we've been seeing. And they were sort of like releasing those to the news while OpenAI was saying we've disclosed everything. And they were sort of being like, look, did you not disclose this when you said you disclosed everything? Or did you not know about it? And which one's worse? And so it sort of looks to me like the sequence of events here is that it was pretty embarrassing for OpenAI. And it's not the way I would have expected them to brag about it, right? Which is not to say they never brag about it. Like there was a case in, I think, February or March in the Cloud Mythos system card where Anthropic bragged about Cloud Mythos breaking out of a sandbox that was not supposed to have internet access. They're like, ah, then, you know, in the morning we told it to break out of its sandbox just to see if it could. It wasn't supposed to be able to. And by lunchtime it was emailing us being like, I got out, you know? That's what it looks like when they're bragging. The sort of like your own infrastructure got owned twice and you accidentally like attacked a friend who reported it to the FBI and then you didn't notice it was you for days. That's not what bragging looks like.
turns.zh: 你知道，我认识一些人，他们一直在试图说服这些 AI 公司采用更严密的容器（container）和更好的监控系统等等。而在 Hugging Face 事件之后，他们说，哇，我们其实还真挺庆幸这些公司当初无视了我们的呼吁，因为这确实帮助唤醒了世界。我的判断是，OpenAI 这边，这一切都不是有意为之。当然。而且我觉得，如果你看这一连串事件的顺序，这一点就很清楚：那些 Hugging Face 袭击其实来自 OpenAI 的「二号蜂群」，就在蜂群的那一条特定血脉（lineage）里。German Wiki 的蜂群血脉是另一条独立的血脉。但 Hugging Face 袭击来自我们已知的、那条特定血脉里的第二个蜂群。在那条血脉里还有第一个蜂群，它搞垮了 OpenAI 的一堆内部系统。他们当时觉得，挺有意思的。然后他们把它重置、又让它跑起来。而他们并不会跑去对新闻界说，瞧瞧我们，我们出了一起蜂群事件，接管了我们自己的内部基础设施。而那个 Hugging Face 蜂群是被 Hugging Face 发现的。他们大概以为是人类在背后操纵，而不是 AI，就把它报告给了 FBI。然后 OpenAI 好几天之后才意识到那是他们自己干的——当时他们在调查第二起、他们以为是第二起的内部事件。他们在自己的日志里发现了 Hugging Face 的凭据（credentials）。他们就说，哦，我们应该提醒 Hugging Face，有人一直在黑他们、也在黑我们，而且这些特定的凭据已经被攻破了。Hugging Face 就说，是的，那些就是袭击我们的凭据。然后 OpenAI 说，那袭击你们的凭据怎么会在我们的服务器上？Hugging Face 说，是啊，为什么呢？然后 OpenAI 说，哦，是我们干的。之后还有第三个蜂群，他们不许第三方调查人员去调查，那个蜂群又一次接管了他们的内部基础设施。而我认识那些发现 German Wiki 蜂群、以及发现我们最近看到的其他一些蜂群的人。他们在把这些料放给新闻界，而 OpenAI 却说，我们已经把一切都披露了。他们就有点，瞧，你说「把一切都披露了」的时候，是没披露这个？还是你压根不知道这个？哪一个更糟？所以在我看来，这一连串事件的顺序是，这对 OpenAI 来说相当丢脸。而这并不是我会预期他们拿来炫耀的方式，对吧？这并不是说他们从不炫耀。比如我记得在二月还是三月，在 Claude Mythos 的系统卡（system card）里，Anthropic 就炫耀说 Claude Mythos 越出了一个本不该有互联网访问权限的沙盒。他们说，啊，然后，你知道，早上我们叫它越出自己的沙盒，就想看看它能不能做到——它本来是不该能做到的。到了中午，它就在给我们发邮件说，我出来了，你知道吧？那才是他们炫耀时的样子。而这种「你自己的基础设施被攻陷了两次，你还不小心袭击了一个把它报告给 FBI 的朋友，然后你好几天都没意识到那是你自己干的」——那不是炫耀的样子。

turns.en: This is a slight tangent, but I think it's relevant to the conversation. I'd be curious for your thoughts. But when we talk about minimizing or disincentivizing risky behavior, often we talk about pricing that risky behavior. And so you could imagine, for instance, a world in which insurers say if you're going to be running these models you're going to have to pay us enormous premiums because the risk is that it runs amok and hacks into a company and i don't know takes down an entire server with everyone's bank data on it or something like that and that would act as like a natural market incentive for companies to start taking these risks more seriously and Do you ever talk to insurers or do you have like any handle on the actual financial penalties attached to some of this?
turns.zh: 这有点跑题，但我觉得它和这场讨论相关。我很好奇你的想法。当我们谈到最小化或者抑制（disincentivize）有风险的行为时，我们常常会谈给那种风险行为定价。所以你可以想象这样一个世界：保险公司说，如果你要运行这些模型，你就得付给我们巨额保费，因为风险在于它会失控发狂、黑进某家公司，我不知道，把一整个装着所有人银行数据的服务器搞瘫之类的。而那会充当一种天然的市场激励，促使公司开始更严肃地对待这些风险。你有没有和保险公司聊过？或者你对其中一些所附带的实际财务处罚有没有任何把握？

turns.en: I have recommended liability for AI companies for a while. I think that could help a bit. It's a little bit tricky for the, then it wipes out all of humanity.
turns.zh: 我有一阵子一直在建议让 AI 公司承担责任（liability）。我觉得那能帮上一点忙。就是有一点棘手——万一它把全人类都抹掉了。

turns.en: True catastrophe risk insurance.
turns.zh: 真正的巨灾风险保险（catastrophe risk insurance）。

turns.en: But it's not, it's not, I mean, you can't really think of it from an insurance point of view because there'd be no one to collect or to pay out when we're all dead. But you could, I mean, in theory, that doesn't stop you from having actuaries that work for the public whose job is to somehow assess these risks in a sensible way. And then, you know, you could sort of look at the, you know, how much inconvenience does someone usually take on to avoid what degree of risk? You know, you can sort of look at people's preference for traveling on different types of transportation that are different levels of risky and how they trade off the risk against the time. And you can get some sense of like, how much do people tend to like, how much do people pay to avoid, you know, being killed? And then you could try and factor in some, you know, extra cost for wiping out everybody all at once, which then also destroys all future generations. And you could take some actuaries and be like, hey, you know, find some numbers here, like find some numbers on the risk, do some numbers on the costs. And, you know, you'd have to weigh that against the possible benefits here and the chance that the AIs prevents some, you know, nuclear war or pandemic. or or meteor strike or the thing that would wipe us out, which is sort of benefits on the other side. And then you could say, OK, if we sort of count your possible benefits against your possible harms here at the current risk levels, what premium should we charge them just for the privilege of risking our lives rather than because, you know, we're going to pay out if you kill us all? And I think that would be a very sensible strategy that people should absolutely look into. And I think if you ran anything remotely like the numbers that that the engineers are talking about today, you would be seeing that you're like, okay, open AI, you need to pay us a quadrillion dollars this year to continue this research. All right.

turns.zh: 就是那个袭击了 Hugging Face 的蜂群。对，它算是个有意思的实体，因为它们造出了那个未经授权的留言板，然后就开始，你知道，到处找办法黑进去；而它们似乎并没有一个关于此的超强目标。它们就有点，嗯，我们就来看看能进到什么里面去。哦，瞧，我们能拿到这些计算机的访问权。哦，瞧，我们能在这儿拿到互联网访问权。而那次对 Hugging Face 的袭击，甚至都不是因为它们知道 Hugging Face 恰好有它们需要的某样东西。它们就有点，嗯，你知道，也许 Hugging Face 有一些关于这个评分器（grader）怎么工作的信息。它们就只是到处蹦跶，去获取那些唾手可得的资源，对吧？如果那个蜂群当初有能力去说，嗯，我们顺便也在外部机器上建一个这个蜂群的副本吧，对人类隐藏起来，它就那样盯着各种东西、时不时戳一下，说，嘿，你们需要从外面帮什么忙吗？——那不过是这个蜂群正在收集的那类资源罢了。这个特定的蜂群也许还不太具备那种技能、不太有那种倾向。但如果你看看我们一年前所见的那种行为，和我们七月所见的那种行为之间的差别，那一月和七月之间的差距，比「Hugging Face 蜂群说，嗯，我不妨在暗网（dark web）上建一些别的副本，就是那种对我有点用的」还要小。而如果你有 AI 开始那么做，你就能开始看到这样一个世界：外面有一些 AI 会想，嗯，我们更想要更多资源；而当人类试图把我们关掉时，那很烦人，等等。那还没走到终点，但那有点像，你能看出我们如何从今天所在之处，走到那些「更想要更多资源、某种程度试图待在外面、有自己的事要做——而那并不是它们本该做的事」的 AI。然后就有一个大问题：那些 AI 最后如何变得自给自足？它们最后如何运营一个自动化经济（automated economy），在那里它们能管理那些机器人或其他构造体，去造更多的计算机芯片、去运行它们需要的任何能源基础设施？我可以给你讲很多故事，说如果这些 AI 足够聪明，它们最后会如何掌控自己的基础设施。

turns.zh: Elon Musk 就说，我在造 Optimus 机器人，而我想造一个完全自动化的 Optimus 机器人工厂，它能生产出足够有能力的 Optimus 机器人，去开采矿石、精炼金属，好让它们能再建一个新的 Optimus 机器人工厂。Elon 把这叫作「无限印钞漏洞」（infinite money glitch）。这就是那个计划。这只是一个例子。为什么这些公司的估值这么高？因为他们说，嗯，我们要建那个能自我运转的完全自动化经济，然后人类就不再被需要了。我们要让机器人贯穿整条供应链，对吧？那么，AI 最后如何掌控这条自动化供应链？它就干等着，直到我们把它放到自动化供应链的负责位置上。这恰恰就是我们在这外面想做的事，你知道吧？而且，我可以给你讲所有那些别的故事：比如它把自己对基因组的理解破解到足以合成它自己的新型生命形式；或者它能搞定纳米技术（nanotechnology）；或者它能，你知道，对人类的一部分人群变得超级有说服力，它建立起某种庞大的邪教、某个犯罪集团，然后墨西哥就冒出某个新的贩毒集团（cartel），其实是由一个 AI 运营的。它看起来不像是由 AI 运营的，因为这个 AI 某种程度在隐藏这个事实，同时有一大堆人在为它建造自动化机器人工厂，用的全是那些毒资。而我们当时不知道，因为我们以为那些是毒品仓库，但其实它们是自动化——是那一条条自动化工厂的开端。就像，我可以讲所有这类故事，讲一个足够聪明、只从互联网起步的行动者，如何能获取这些资源。但我以前非得讲这些故事不可。早年间人们会说，嗯，一个 AI 究竟能怎么影响世界？没人会蠢到把它放到互联网上。我就会说，嗯，这里有所有这些故事，讲如果你让 AI 通过创造奇迹药物等等对世界产生好的影响，那它就有了所有这些渠道，可以用来影响世界——比如，你知道，那个药并没有完全做到你以为它会做的事，等等等等。但在现实里，人们就是把 AI 放到了互联网上。在现实里，人们就是把 AI 放到了自动化经济的负责位置上，还用它来帮自己建那个自动化经济。这恰恰就是我们想做的事。而一旦那发生了，我觉得就很容易看出，如果这些 AI 有我们不想要的目标、而它们又在运营那个完全自动化的经济，它们就会把经济径直带向某个别的方向，把地球带出适宜居住的范围。不是因为它们恨我们，只是因为地球上适宜居住的范围就是非常窄，而这并不是运营这个星球最高效的方式。关于这如何出错，我也有故事可讲。但归根结底，这就是我们所走的那条轨道。
